name_en: Bandai Mochi — firm rice pounded on a board, from Nikko's Kuriyama district
summary_ja: 日光市栗山地区に伝わる、うるち米を硬めに炊いてつく餅。山小屋の板の上で斧の峰などで叩いてついたことから「板台餅」と呼ばれ、味噌だれやあんこ、じゅうねなど地域ごとの食べ方が残る。
summary_en: In the Kuriyama district of Nikko, firm-cooked non-glutinous rice is pounded on a wooden board — hence 'itadai-mochi,' board-mochi — and eaten with miso glaze, sweet bean paste, or a perilla-seed sauce depending on the hamlet.
source_title: 板台餅／ばんだい餅 栃木県

name_en: Komugi Manju — steamed wheat buns filled with sweet bean paste
summary_ja: 重曹を加えた小麦粉の生地であんを包んで蒸したまんじゅう。麦の収穫が終わったばかりの盆の時期に欠かせない菓子で、地獄の蓋が開くとされる旧暦7月1日には先祖に供える習わしもある。
summary_en: Wheat dough leavened with baking soda wraps sweet bean paste and is steamed — a treat tied to the Obon season just after the wheat harvest, once offered to ancestors on the old-calendar day the gates of the underworld were said to open.
source_title: 小麦まんじゅう 栃木県

name_en: Botamochi — pounded rice topped with sweet bean paste for equinox and Obon
summary_ja: うるち米ともち米を炊いて丸め、あんをのせた餅菓子。春秋の彼岸や盆に欠かせず、稲刈りや脱穀の後にこぼれた米でつくる「刈りあげぼた餅」など、収穫の節目を祝う名も残っている。
summary_en: Cooked non-glutinous and glutinous rice is shaped and topped with sweet bean paste — a fixture of spring and autumn equinox and Obon, with names like 'harvest botamochi,' made from rice gleaned after threshing to mark the season's end.

name_en: Kusa Mochi — pounded rice kneaded with young mugwort
summary_ja: 芽吹いたばかりのよもぎを練り込んだ餅。ひな節句に飾り、きな粉などをまぶして食べる風習があり、旧暦での節句を守る土地では餅草の育ち具合を待ってからつくられてきた。
summary_en: Freshly sprouted mugwort is kneaded into pounded rice — displayed at the Doll Festival and eaten dusted with soybean flour, made only once the young mugwort has grown enough in places still keeping to the old lunar calendar.

name_en: Yaki Mochi — leftover rice pan-fried with flour and miso
summary_ja: 残りごはんに小麦粉や味噌を混ぜて丸め、ほうろくやフライパンで焼いた素朴なおやつ。傷みやすい夏のごはんを日持ちさせる知恵でもあり、地域や家庭によって蒸したり茹でたりもする。
summary_en: Leftover rice is mixed with flour and miso, shaped, and pan-fried into a simple snack — a way of keeping quick-to-spoil summer rice edible longer, with some households steaming or boiling it instead.
